topic: Behind a blunt body, wind sheds vortices alternately from each side at a frequency fixed by the Strouhal number, about 0.2, from a 1.5 km island down to a singing wire
summary: When a steady flow passes a bluff obstacle such as a cylinder, an island or a wire, the wake becomes unstable and rolls up into vortices that leave the two sides in turn, clockwise on one edge and counterclockwise on the other. The result is a staggered double row called a von Karman vortex street. Its shedding frequency follows f = St x U / D with St close to 0.2 over a huge range of Reynolds numbers, so the same pattern appears in lab tanks, in cloud decks behind islands hundreds of kilometres long, and as the hum of power lines.

facts.claim: A vortex street forms only within a range of flow speeds, specified by the Reynolds number, typically above a limiting value of about 90; the Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in the flow.
For a cylinder the Strouhal number St = f D / V varies only between 0.18 and 0.22 over four orders of magnitude in Reynolds number, from 100 to 100,000.
The Strouhal number is named after Vincenc Strouhal, a Czech physicist who experimented in 1878 with wires experiencing vortex shedding and singing in the wind.

Behind Alejandro Selkirk Island, about 1.5 km in diameter, a steady wind sheds clockwise vortices off the eastern edge and counterclockwise vortices off the western edge; they grow as they drift hundreds of kilometres downwind, a street 10,000 times longer than lab streets.
facts.source_title: Landsat 7 Reveals Large-scale Fractal Motion of Clouds (NASA Earth Observatory)

facts.claim: MISR images from June 6, 2001 show a vortex pattern continuing for over 300 km south of Jan Mayen island, with cloud-clearing at the vortex centres until the sixteenth hole closes.
facts.source_title: A Vortex Street in the Arctic (NASA Earth Observatory)

facts.claim: In air moving over a cylinder the Aeolian tone has frequency St x V / D with St about 0.2, so each doubling of wind speed raises the tone by an octave, up to a six octave swing in gusty wind.

Tall steel chimneys and masts are fitted with helical strakes to break up shedding; their effectiveness against vortex induced vibration was found in 1957 by Christopher Scruton and D. E. J. Walshe at the National Physical Laboratory.
The Reynolds number compares inertial forces to viscous forces in a flow, so the same flow pattern recurs whenever velocity times length divided by kinematic viscosity matches.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Alternating vortex shedding
visualisable_mechanisms.description: The two shear layers leaving a bluff body roll up in turn: one side releases a clockwise vortex, then the other releases a counterclockwise one, half a period later, forming a staggered double row that drifts downstream.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Tracer particles or dye advected by a small 2D flow past an obstacle; colour by vorticity sign so the two rows alternate in two tones.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Strouhal frequency scaling
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Shedding frequency f equals St x U / D with St near 0.2, so doubling flow speed doubles the shedding rate, and a smaller obstacle sheds faster at the same speed.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Several obstacles of different diameters in one stream shed at visibly different rates; a tone per obstacle at f, one octave up for each doubling of speed.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Reynolds number regime change
visualisable_mechanisms.description: At low Reynolds number the wake stays as two steady bound eddies; above roughly 90 the wake starts to oscillate and shed a regular street; at much higher values the street breaks into turbulence.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Ramp the flow speed over time so the wake moves from a calm closed bubble, to a regular street, to a frayed turbulent wake.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Island cloud street growth
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Behind an island the vortices are carried hundreds of kilometres downwind and grow as they drift, opening clear holes in the stratocumulus deck at their centres.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: A top-down cloud deck with an island obstacle; vortex cores clear holes that widen and fade with downstream distance.

open_questions: Why does the Strouhal number stay so close to 0.2 across four orders of magnitude of Reynolds number?
How far downstream does an atmospheric street keep its regular spacing before mixing erases it?

surprise.justification: Most people know eddies form behind rocks, but few know the shedding rate obeys one nearly constant ratio that links a humming power line to a 300 km cloud pattern behind an Arctic volcano.
